nameStory: The Hairy-necked Tiger Beetle gets its name from the fuzzy hairs that cover its neck area (called the prothorax), giving it a distinctly "hairy" appearance. It's also sometimes called the Moustached Tiger Beetle, since those neck hairs can look like facial hair from certain angles. Like all tiger beetles, it earned the "tiger" part of its name from its fierce predatory nature and striped markings.
description: The Hairy-necked Tiger Beetle is a medium-sized predatory beetle that hunts along sandy beaches and riverbanks throughout New England. These sleek hunters are dark brown with cream or white markings across their wing covers, and they're small enough to sit comfortably on your fingertip at about half an inch long. You'll spot them during summer months as they dart across sand with lightning speed, chasing down smaller insects with their powerful jaws. Despite their small size, they're fierce predators with excellent eyesight and impressive running abilities.

idTips.label: Hairy neck area
idTips.description: Look closely at the area behind the head - it's covered in fine, visible hairs that give the beetle a fuzzy appearance, unlike the smooth necks of most other tiger beetles

idTips.label: Dark brown body
idTips.description: The head, neck, and wing covers are consistently dark brown - almost chocolate colored - with a slight metallic sheen that catches sunlight

idTips.label: Cream markings
idTips.description: Pale cream or white irregular markings stand out boldly against the dark wing covers, creating a distinctive pattern unique to each individual

idTips.label: Medium size
idTips.description: About the length of your pinky nail (roughly half an inch), making it noticeably smaller than a penny but larger than most ants

idTips.label: Sandy habitat preference
idTips.description: Almost always found on or very near sand - beaches, sandy riverbanks, or sand bars - where their coloring helps them blend with the substrate

idTips.label: Lightning-fast movement
idTips.description: Moves in quick bursts across sand, stopping abruptly to look around before darting off again - too fast to follow easily with your eyes

habitat: Look for Hairy-necked Tiger Beetles on sandy beaches along the New England coast, especially where waves have deposited fresh sand bars or created wide sandy flats. They also frequent the sandy banks of rivers and large streams, particularly areas that flood seasonally and leave behind clean sand deposits. You'll have the best luck finding them on warm, sunny days when they're most active hunting.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in late spring as temperatures warm, but they're not yet at peak activity. Look for them on the warmest, sunniest days along sandy shores.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most visible, actively hunting and mating. This is the best time to observe their characteristic fast-paced hunting behavior on sunny beaches and sand bars.
seasonality.fall: Activity decreases as temperatures drop, with adults becoming less common. By late fall, most have completed their life cycle or gone into hiding.
seasonality.winter: Not active during winter months in New England. Adults either die off after reproducing, or larvae develop underground in sandy substrates until the following year.

funFact: Tiger beetles are so fast that they literally run blind - when chasing prey at top speed, they move faster than their eyes can process visual information, so they have to stop periodically to relocate their target before continuing the chase!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other tiger beetles, but the hairy neck is the dead giveaway - run your finger gently over a captured specimen and you'll feel the fuzz. Memory trick: "Hairy-necked needs a haircut" - if you can see or feel hair on the neck area, you've found your beetle.
contextualKnowledge: Tiger beetles are considered indicator species for healthy ecosystems - their presence suggests good environmental conditions. However, the Hairy-necked Tiger Beetle's population is declining, likely due to coastal development and beach disturbance, making each sighting increasingly special.
compareHints: Among New England's tiger beetles, the Hairy-necked is the only one with those distinctive fuzzy neck hairs. The Six-spotted Tiger Beetle is bright metallic green, while the Big Sand Tiger Beetle is much larger and bulkier. The Bronzed Tiger Beetle shares sandy habitats but has a distinctly bronzy-copper color rather than dark brown, and lacks the hairy neck entirely.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's tiger beetles, the six-spotted stands out for its pure metallic green color - the bronzed tiger beetle has more copper tones, while the festive tiger beetle is darker with different spot patterns.

Among New England's tiger beetles, the Bronzed Tiger Beetle is distinguished by its warm copper-bronze coloration, while the Six-spotted Tiger Beetle shines bright metallic green and the Purple Tiger Beetle displays cooler purple-blue tones.
Among New England's tiger beetles, the festive tiger beetle is distinguished by its particular pattern of white markings and metallic coloration.
Among New England's tiger beetles, the twelve-spotted is unique for having exactly twelve spots on a dark body.
Among New England's tiger beetles, the Oblique-lined stands out with its exceptionally large compound eyes and distinctive diagonal white markings.
Among New England's tiger beetles, the Big Sand Tiger Beetle stands out for its robust, chunky build compared to the more slender Six-spotted or Bronzed Tiger Beetles.
Unlike the bright metallic green Six-spotted Tiger Beetle with its obvious white spots, the Purple Tiger Beetle shows deep purple metallic colors without distinct white markings.

Unlike the Six-spotted Tiger Beetle which prefers woodland paths, or the Bronzed Tiger Beetle found on sandy beaches, the Common Claybank Tiger Beetle is the only New England tiger beetle that specializes in clay habitats.
